Nationalism. A political ideology and social movement that emphasizes the interests, identity, and sovereignty of a nation or national group, often viewed as a collective bound by common language, culture, history, territory, or ethnicity. Emerging powerfully in the nineteenth century as a consequence of Enlightenment ideas and the French Revolution, nationalism transformed political life by replacing dynastic loyalty with loyalty to the nation. It became a driving force for both liberation, such as the unification of Italy and Germany and the decolonization movements, and also for imperialism, rivalry among powers, and eventually world war. Nationalism persists as one of the most potent forces in international relations and domestic politics. Before modern times, political allegiance was primarily to dynasties and religious institutions. Nationalism redirected loyalty toward imagined communities bound by national identity, creating the modern nation-state as a primary political unit. The French Revolution and Napoleon Bonaparte were pivotal moments. While Napoleon's military dominance imposed French law and administration across Europe, it actually sparked counter-nationalist movements as conquered peoples asserted national identity against foreign domination. Romantic nationalism in the nineteenth century emphasized the unique character, spirit, and genius of each nation. Intellectuals celebrated folk traditions, national languages, and historical narratives as expressions of distinct national essence. Nationalism became the ideological fuel for unification movements. Italy was unified through the efforts of Cavour and Garibaldi, and Germany through Bismarck, as nationalist fervor consolidated powerful nation-states from fragmented regions and dynasties. Yet imperialism was often justified through nationalism as powerful nations claimed superiority and destiny to dominate others, framing conquest as civilizing missions. Nationalism thus became an engine of imperial expansion and colonialism. The Mexican Revolution from 1910 to 1920 was partly driven by nationalism, as revolutionaries asserted Mexican control over Mexican resources and destiny against foreign economic domination and internal elitism. In the realm of sport, nationalism manifests as national pride in athletic competition. The Olympic Games became an arena for nations to compete and display superiority, often weaponized during the Cold War. Nationalism contributed directly to world wars. National rivalries, imperial competition, and mutual distrust among nationalist powers fueled the geopolitical tensions that exploded into World War I and World War II. After World War II, decolonization movements invoked nationalism to justify independence from European empires. Formerly colonized peoples claimed national self-determination and sovereignty based on nationalist ideology.
